summaries.gardner: CME fits only a few Rule Breaker traits: it is the top dog in futures with benchmark contracts and the most valuable exchange brand, but futures trading is a mature industry rather than an emerging one. The shares rose 14.06% over the past 52 weeks (about 17.9% with dividends), modestly ahead of the S&P 500, and while some analysts (Goldman Sachs, Sell) call it expensive, it is not widely seen as an overvalued high-flier.
summaries.buffett: CME has many Buffett traits: a simple toll-booth business with a wide moat, a 64.9% operating margin in 2025, free cash flow of $4,193.6 million (2025) and almost all earnings paid out as regular plus annual variable dividends. The main drawback is price: at about 25 times trailing earnings and a free-cash-flow yield under 4%, it is a wonderful business at a full price rather than a bargain.
summaries.munger: Inverting, there are few ways CME's franchise could fail: its benchmark contracts and integrated clearing house create strong network effects that rivals such as FMX have struggled to break. Risks are regulation, prediction-market and crypto-native competitors and lower volatility, and the valuation (about 25 times earnings) leaves little room for error, which Munger would accept only for an outstanding business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would call CME a stalwart with an easy story: more trading in rates, equities, energy and metals means more fees. But its P/E of about 25 is well above its EPS growth (diluted EPS rose from $7.40 in 2022 to $11.16 in 2025, about 15% a year, with lower growth expected), insiders are selling, and it is widely followed, so it fails his PEG and overlooked tests.
summaries.fisher: CME keeps launching new products (micro contracts, crypto futures, tungsten and European dairy futures, U.S. Treasury clearing, the FanDuel prediction-market venture) and has expanded operating margin from 54.0% in 2020 to 64.9% in 2025. It does not report R&D, its revenue growth is moderate (about 9% a year in 2022-2025), and its strength is more market structure than sales or research excellence, so it fits Fisher's points only in part.
summaries.graham: CME passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability, dividend record (paid every year since 2003) and EPS growth tests (diluted EPS from $3.69 in 2015 to $11.16 in 2025). It fails the valuation tests badly: the price is about 31 times three-year average EPS and P/E times P/B is about 104, far above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: CME is a near-monopoly in U.S. benchmark futures, which Thiel would admire, with durable network effects and its own distribution through clearing firms and CME Globex. But it is a 1898-rooted incumbent without a 10x proprietary technology or a secret new market, so it fits the monopoly questions better than the zero-to-one questions.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with disciplined management; CME offers durability, very high margins and steady 9% revenue growth in the first nine months of 2026, but at about 24 times forward earnings and a PEG well above 1 the price is full. It benefits from volatility and rising government debt rather than from the AI platform shift he focuses on.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and macro tailwinds; CME's adjusted EPS rose 12.7% in Q3 2026 with record Q3 volume of 29.4 million contracts a day, and volatility, heavy Treasury issuance and the SEC Treasury clearing mandate are tailwinds. Growth is steady rather than explosive, so it looks more like a defensive holding than a concentrated high-conviction bet.
summaries.smith: CME suits much of Terry Smith's approach: very high margins, strong cash conversion (free cash flow of $4,193.6 million vs net income of $4,021.0 million in 2025), modest debt and a durable franchise. The weak points are a return on equity of only about 15-16% because of large merger goodwill, limited reinvestment opportunities and a valuation near 25 times earnings, so it fits 'good company' better than 'don't overpay'.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula CME scores well on return on tangible capital but poorly on earnings yield: trailing operating income of about $4.58 billion is only about 4% of its roughly $111 billion enterprise value. It would be unlikely to rank highly in a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: CME passes Akre's first leg (an extraordinary business with a 64.9% operating margin and a wide moat) and partly the second (long-tenured, capable management, with Lynne Fitzpatrick due to succeed Terry Duffy as CEO on March 1, 2027). It largely fails the third leg because it pays out almost all its earnings as dividends rather than reinvesting at high rates.
summaries.pabrai: CME is a low-risk, high-quality business with little chance of permanent loss, but there is no temporary setback or deep discount that would create a Dhandho-style 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bet at about 25 times earnings. Pabrai would likely see it as a good business at a full price.
summaries.wood: CME is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator; it is an incumbent exchange, though it is a leading venue for regulated bitcoin and ether futures and is building 24/7 crypto trading and retail prediction markets. Its addressable market is unlikely to grow many times over in five years.
summaries.ackman: CME closely matches Ackman's stated criteria of a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with a dominant market position and high barriers to entry, and it carries modest debt. The missing element is price: at about 25 times earnings there is no obvious discount to intrinsic value or activist catalyst.
summaries.sleep: CME has scale advantages but tends to keep them rather than share them, regularly raising fees (for example up to 3.5% increases in 2027 market data and licence fees). It therefore fits Nick Sleep's durable-franchise ideas more than his scale-economies-shared model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with great technology; CME is a mature, long-established exchange group, so it falls largely outside his approach, though its markets solve a large, painful problem (price risk) for a huge customer base.
summaries.nash: On Tom Nash's checks CME scores well on quality (operating margin about 66%, short interest 1.57%, institutional ownership 91.1%, revenue growing faster than expenses) and totals about 80 on his 13-category scale. But it fails his instant-kill test because debt ($3,425.1 million) exceeded cash ($2,198.5 million) at September 30, 2026, revenue growth is below 10% (9.3% in the first nine months of 2026), and his DCF value (about $175 a share) is well below the $307.04 price.

momentum.evidence: CME rose 14.06% over 52 weeks to $307.04 on Oct 26, 2026 (about 17.9% total return with dividends), modestly ahead of the S&P 500 ETF SPY's 14.23% one-year total return.

g4.evidence: Terry Duffy has led CME as chairman since 2002 and CEO since 2017, with CFO Lynne Fitzpatrick named to succeed him on March 1, 2027; it is 91.1% institutionally owned but has no famous investor or partner championing it, apart from Google Cloud as technology partner.

g6.evidence: Some analysts call it expensive (Goldman Sachs rates it Sell with a $271 target), but the 17-analyst consensus is Buy with a $316 target, close to the price.

simple.evidence: CME earns fees on futures and options contracts traded and cleared on its exchanges plus market data fees, a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose from $3,326.8 million in 2015 to $6,520.6 million in 2025 and the company has been profitable every year, with four consecutive record revenue years through 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management returns excess cash through an annual variable dividend ($6.15 a share paid in March 2026) and reports candidly, but CEO Terry Duffy sold 35,000 shares ($10.4 million) in May 2026 and the board has a history of exchange-member director seats.

b6.evidence: CME grew through big deals (CBOT and NYMEX in 2007-2008, NEX Group in 2018) but has since focused on organic products, Treasury clearing and partnerships rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: Operating margin is very high (64.9% in 2025) and debt is modest ($3,425.1 million), but large merger goodwill ($10,505.9 million) keeps return on equity at about 16% and ROIC at 12.55% (StockAnalysis).

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $4,193.6 million in 2025 (operating cash flow $4,277.1 million less $83.5 million of capex), slightly above net income of $4,021.0 million.

b10.evidence: CME pays out nearly all its earnings (dividends paid of $3,933.0 million in 2025 vs net income of $4,021.0 million), and the little it keeps has gone with a rise in market value from about $77 billion to about $110 billion over five years.

safety.evidence: At $307.04 the stock trades at about 25 times trailing EPS and above a simple DCF value of about $175 a share using a 12% discount rate, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of 25.18 and forward P/E of 23.72 are full for revenue growth of about 9% a year, though arguably reasonable for a near-monopoly with a 64.9% operating margin.

mu5.evidence: Failure paths are few: its benchmark contracts, integrated clearing house and margin offsets (about $100 billion a day in Q3 2026) make it hard to displace, with regulation and new venues like FMX the main risks.

reinvest.evidence: CME needs little capital (capex of $83.5 million in 2025) and returns nearly all earnings as dividends, so it cannot reinvest large sums at high returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: a dominant exchange whose fees grow with trading volume, record 2025 ADV of 28.1 million contracts and new products.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 25 is well above EPS growth of about 15% a year from 2022 ($7.40) to 2025 ($11.16) and analysts' expected growth near 10%.

runway.evidence: Growth can continue through Treasury clearing, international clients, retail and crypto products, but core futures revenue grows at a mid-to-high single-digit pace (6.4% in 2025, 9.3% in the first nine months of 2026).

ly7.evidence: CEO Terry Duffy sold 35,000 shares in May 2026 with no insider buying reported, and diluted shares edged up from 358.5 million in 2020 to 360.3 million in 2025 before a $524 million Q3 2026 buyback cut them to 358.6 million.

ly8.evidence: CME is followed by about 17 analysts and is 91.1% owned by institutions, so it is not overlooked, though exchanges are a 'boring' niche.

fi2.evidence: CME keeps adding products as markets mature, such as micro contracts, crypto futures (bitcoin cash and Uniswap in October 2026), tungsten futures, European dairy futures and Treasury clearing.

fi3.evidence: CME does not report R&D spending; its product and technology investment (including the Google Cloud migration) has produced record volumes, but results are hard to tie to research outlays.

fi4.evidence: Its global sales teams have grown non-U.S. activity to record levels (record non-U.S. ADV in Q3 2026), but its growth comes mainly from liquidity and market demand rather than unusual selling skill.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in long-term projects such as the Google Cloud partnership and Treasury clearing, but it also pays out nearly all earnings each year, reflecting a strong short-term shareholder-return focus.

gr1.evidence: CME is a large company with a market value of about $110 billion and 2025 revenue of $6,520.6 million.

ni10.evidence: Net income was positive every year from 2016 ($1,534.1 million) to 2025 ($4,021.0 million).

gr4.evidence: CME has paid dividends every year since 2003, 23 consecutive years through 2025.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.69 in 2015 to $11.16 in 2025, roughly tripling.

th1.evidence: CME's advantage is liquidity and benchmark ownership rather than technology ten times better than rivals; it is moving its platform onto Google Cloud.
